subject: economics
topicDisplay: Individuals Firms Markets And Market Failure
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A monopolist that practises first-degree (perfect) price discrimination:
options: Charges every consumer their maximum willingness to pay, capturing all consumer surplus
questions.explain: Perfect price discrimination charges each consumer their reservation price, converting all consumer surplus into profit.

questions.q: A market is described as a contestable market when:
options: There are very high barriers to entry and exit
There is a single dominant firm only
Barriers to entry and exit are low and there is a threat of new entrants
questions.explain: Contestable markets have low entry and exit barriers, so the threat of hit-and-run entry disciplines incumbents.

questions.q: Regulatory capture is an example of government failure in which:
options: A regulator comes to serve the interests of the firms it is supposed to regulate
Regulators act in the public interest at all times
questions.explain: Regulatory capture occurs when the regulating body is dominated by the industry's interests rather than protecting consumers.

questions.q: A negative production externality exists when:
options: Marginal private cost exceeds marginal social cost
Marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit
Marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost
Marginal private benefit equals marginal social benefit
questions.explain: A negative production externality means the cost to society (MSC) is greater than the private cost borne by the firm (MPC), creating a divergence equal to the external cost.

questions.q: Collusion between oligopolists to fix prices is an example of:
options: A cartel acting to raise joint profits
questions.explain: Colluding firms form a cartel to restrict output and raise prices, behaving like a monopoly to boost profit.

questions.q: Which point on an externality diagram shows the socially optimal level of output?
questions.explain: Allocative efficiency is achieved where marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit, the social optimum.

questions.q: The Gini coefficient is a measure of:
questions.explain: The Gini coefficient summarises the degree of income (or wealth) inequality, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).

questions.q: An indirect tax used to correct a negative externality should ideally be set equal to:
options: The marginal external cost at the socially optimal output
questions.explain: A Pigouvian tax internalises the externality by being set equal to the marginal external cost at the social optimum, aligning MPC with MSC.

questions.q: At the free-market equilibrium for a good with a negative consumption externality, the market produces:
options: The quantity where MSC equals zero
More than the social optimum, creating a welfare loss
questions.explain: Because MPB exceeds MSB, the market over-consumes relative to where MSB equals MSC, generating a deadweight welfare loss.

questions.q: A key feature distinguishing monopolistic competition from perfect competition is:
options: A single firm in the market
Product differentiation giving a downward-sloping demand curve
questions.explain: In monopolistic competition firms sell differentiated products, giving each a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.q: An indirect tax on a good with very price-inelastic demand will mainly:
options: Raise significant tax revenue with only a small fall in quantity
questions.explain: With inelastic demand, quantity changes little, so the tax is effective at raising revenue but less effective at cutting consumption.

questions.q: A key limitation of using indirect taxes to correct externalities is that:
options: It is difficult to place an accurate monetary value on the external cost
questions.explain: Valuing externalities precisely is difficult, so the tax may be set too high or too low, risking government failure.

questions.q: Diseconomies of scale are most commonly caused by:
options: Spreading fixed costs over more units
Problems of coordination, communication and control as a firm grows
questions.explain: As firms grow very large, managerial and communication difficulties raise long-run average cost.

questions.q: The deadweight welfare loss from a negative production externality is the area:
options: Between MSC and MPC, between the free-market and socially optimal outputs
Above the supply curve at zero output
questions.explain: The welfare loss triangle lies between the MSC and MPC curves over the range of over-production beyond the social optimum.

questions.q: Productive efficiency for a firm occurs where:
options: Output is produced at the minimum point of the average cost curve
questions.explain: Productive efficiency is achieved when output is produced at the lowest point of the average cost curve.

questions.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost in the short run?
questions.explain: Rent does not vary with output in the short run, making it a fixed cost.

questions.q: A firm maximises profit at the level of output where:
options: Total revenue is at a maximum
questions.explain: Profit is maximised where MC=MR, because beyond this point an extra unit adds more to cost than to revenue.

questions.q: Internal economies of scale that arise from spreading research and design costs over a larger output are called:
questions.explain: Technical economies include spreading large indivisible costs such as R&D and capital over greater output.

questions.q: A pure public good is best defined as one that is:
options: Provided only by the government and free at the point of use
questions.explain: A pure public good is simultaneously non-rival (one person's use does not diminish another's) and non-excludable (people cannot be prevented from consuming it).

questions.q: A subsidy granted to producers of a good with positive externalities shifts the:
options: Supply curve to the right, lowering price and increasing output toward the social optimum
Supply curve to the left, raising price
questions.explain: A producer subsidy lowers costs, shifting supply right so output rises toward the optimum where MSB equals MSC.

questions.q: Government failure occurs when intervention:
options: Increases consumer surplus without any cost
Results in a net welfare loss or a misallocation of resources
questions.explain: Government failure arises when state intervention causes a more inefficient allocation of resources than would have existed otherwise.

questions.q: State provision of a good free at the point of use can lead to government failure through:
options: A reduction in the budget deficit
Excess demand, queues and possible over-consumption owing to zero price
questions.explain: Providing a good at zero price can encourage over-consumption and rationing problems such as waiting lists, a form of government failure.

questions.q: Net migration of skilled workers into a country will tend to:
options: Have no effect on the labour market
Always raise wages for all workers
Shift labour supply right and reduce upward wage pressure in affected occupations
questions.explain: An inflow of workers increases labour supply, shifting the supply curve right and easing wage growth where they compete.

questions.q: A quasi-public good differs from a pure public good because it:
options: Has the potential to be made excludable or is partly rival
questions.explain: Quasi-public goods (e.g. a beach or a road) only partially satisfy non-rivalry and non-excludability and can sometimes be made excludable.

questions.q: A positive consumption externality means that, at the free-market equilibrium, society:
options: Under-consumes the good relative to the social optimum
questions.explain: When MSB exceeds MPB, the market under-consumes because consumers ignore the external benefits, justifying a subsidy.

questions.q: A natural monopoly is characterised by:
options: High and continuous economies of scale so one firm supplies the market at lowest cost
questions.explain: Natural monopolies have such large economies of scale that a single firm can supply the whole market most cheaply.

questions.q: A key advantage of tradable pollution permits over a fixed tax is that they:
options: Require no government involvement at all
Always raise more revenue than a carbon tax
Guarantee a precise total quantity of pollution while allowing the market to set the price
questions.explain: A cap-and-trade scheme fixes the aggregate quantity of emissions and lets the permit price emerge from trading, ensuring an environmental target is met.

questions.q: Average total cost equals:
options: The change in total cost from one more unit
questions.explain: Average total cost is total cost divided by the quantity of output produced.

questions.q: Which factor would shift the demand for labour curve to the right?
options: A rise in the wage rate
An increase in capital that substitutes for labour
An increase in the demand for the firm's product
A fall in the price of the product
questions.explain: Since labour demand is derived, a rise in product demand raises MRP and shifts the labour demand curve rightward.

questions.q: The Coase theorem suggests that externalities can be resolved efficiently if:
options: The government always intervenes with taxes
Property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low
questions.explain: Coase argued that with well-defined property rights and negligible bargaining costs, private parties can negotiate an efficient outcome without government.
